newsitem.title: USA: Orange County DA seeks 7-year term for ex-treasurer.
newsitem.headline: Orange County DA seeks 7-year term for ex-treasurer.

text.p: The former treasurer of California's Orange County should serve seven years in prison for crimes stemming from the largest municipal bankruptcy in U.S. history, the county district attorney said on Tuesday.

In court papers filed in Santa Ana, Orange County District Attorney Michael Capizzi also recommended that former Treasurer Robert Citron be fined $400,000. The papers were released in advance of Citron's sentencing hearing on Nov. 18.
The county filed for bankruptcy protection Dec. 6, 1994, after sustaining losses of more than $1.6 billion on risky investments. The county emerged from bankruptcy last June.
Citron, widely blamed for the financial crisis, pleaded guilty last year to several counts of securities fraud and misappropriation of funds. He faces up to 14 years in prison.
"Since his plea, defendant (Citron) has been candid, truthful and accommodating -- as he agreed to be at the time he plead guilty," the district attorney said.

Capizzi added, however, that Citron's "crimes and the financial damage caused by him are too serious to justify a probation grant," and if one-half of Citron's monthly income were paid as a fine, the entire fine could be satisfied within 10 years, he said.
"In the people's view, a penal fine of $400,000, in addition to the prescribed term of imprisonment, would be appropriate punishment for the crimes committed," Capizzi said in court papers.
Citron attorney David Wiechert called the district attorney's recommendations "incredibly harsh."
Wiechert said Citron should receive probation and a fine of $10,000. If any confinement were to be required, his client should only receive home detention, Wiechert argued.
In court papers, Wiechert painted a tragic portrait of Citron as a man who had lost everything and was viewed by the public as a pariah.

"The privacy and intimacy he once shared with his wife in their modest home has been shattered by glaring TV cameras and trash scrounging reporters," he said. "A prison term would take away the last vestiges of Mr. Citron's reason for being."

Wiechert also said Citron's "mental limitations caught up with him (and that his) psychological deficits rendered him susceptible to the advice of trusted counselors," such as investment giant Merrill Lynch & Co..
Wiechert released psychological evaluations indicating that Citron was "seriously impaired" in executive functioning, a key part of his job as county treasurer.
Merrill Lynch maintains that Citron was an experienced and sophisticated treasurer who made his own investment decisions.
